list.sentence: Foreign Information Program, , , > But American policy toward China, which they conceive to be the product of a stupid or wicked government rather than the will of the American people, is heartily condemned by all student liberals. — , The overseas Chinese analysis is , China, : restraint and exchange The opening to Peking made the information agencies weigh what not to say as well as what to show: before the President's visit officials wanted to seem neither soft on Communism nor hostile to Peking, and proposed to turn a temporary psychological asset into a lasting one; by the the American mission in Peking saw a real, if revocable, chance to widen communication. > While we do not want to appear as having gone “soft” on Chinese Communism neither do we want to appear anti-Chinese or anti-Peking. — , > The President’s projected visit to Peking presents us with opportunities to build what is now a temporary psychological asset into a long-range one. — , > But the Chinese appear to be determined to go down this road, and until the line changes—which it can do although at considerable cost—we have an opportunity to enhance the communication process to a significant degree. — , ## How this was done Because *soft power* is a term of , the run first read the FRUS editors' own chapter headings (about 25,000 of them, of which about 150 bore on the subject) to learn the period's words — information policy, the foreign information programme, public diplomacy, cultural relations — and then searched the full text of all 553 FRUS volumes, of which it used 84: the regional East Asia and Pacific volumes for and the eight volumes on the information programme and public diplomacy.
